story.title: Trump Gave $45,000 Holiday Gifts to Aides, Financial Disclosures Reveal
story.summary: Donald Trump provided $45,000 holiday gifts to Natalie Harp and two other White House aides, as detailed in recent financial disclosures. This amount was categorized as 'cash gift for the holidays' and was in addition to their regular salaries. The practice of giving such gifts has been described as longstanding by a White House spokesperson.

explore_lenses.label: What do the disclosures show beyond $45,000?
explore_lenses.title: Four aides reported $155,000 total
explore_lenses.summary: The reported $45,000 payments were three separate holiday gifts, not one shared amount. A fourth White House aide, Walt Nauta, disclosed a $20,000 holiday gift.

claims.text: Natalie Harp’s OGE Form 278e identifies Donald J. Trump of Palm Beach, Florida, as the source of a $45,000 “Cash gift for the holidays.”
ABC News reported that Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris each disclosed the same $45,000 amount, while Nauta disclosed $20,000, for $155,000 across the four aides.
The reported gifts were separate from the aides’ White House pay: ABC reported $150,000 salaries for Harp, Martin, and Harris and $175,000 for Nauta.

explore_lenses.label: Do federal ethics rules allow such gifts?
explore_lenses.title: The key issue is whether they were gifts or pay
explore_lenses.summary: Rules governing gifts between federal employees expressly permit a subordinate to accept a gift from an official superior. A separate criminal statute bars private salary supplementation when it is compensation for government service, making the purpose of the payments legally consequential.

claims.text: The executive-branch ethics regulation says an employee may accept a gift from an employee who is the recipient’s official superior; it defines “official superior” to exclude the President and Vice President.
18 U.S.C. § 209 prohibits an executive-branch employee from receiving private salary or salary supplementation as compensation for government service.

White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said the payments had no connection to the aides’ official duties, were gifts rather than compensation, and were permissible under applicable legal and ethical standards.

explore_lenses.label: Who received the gifts, and why are they notable?
explore_lenses.title: They went to close Oval Office aides
explore_lenses.summary: The recipients include aides with daily operational, communications, and executive-assistant roles around Trump. The payments drew attention because of their size and because several recipients have long worked for him in government, campaigns, or private settings.

claims.text: Harp’s disclosure identifies her as special assistant and executive assistant to the president, appointed in January 2025 as non-career executive-branch personnel.

CBS described Martin as a communications adviser, Harris as deputy director of Oval Office Operations, and Nauta as director of Oval Office Operations; it reported that all have longstanding ties to Trump.
Sen. Jon Ossoff, a Georgia Democrat, had separately criticized Trump’s attention to projects and travel involving Harp; the White House did not connect that criticism to the gifts.

story_report.summary: Financial disclosures show that President Donald Trump gave cash holiday gifts to several White House aides, including a $45,000 gift reported by Natalie Harp. ABC News reported that Margo Martin and Chamberlain Harris each disclosed $45,000 and Walt Nauta disclosed $20,000, totaling $155,000 among the four aides. The payments were reported separately from their White House salaries, making the disclosures a public record of the gifts and their stated values.

sections.heading: Disclosures identify recipients and roles
sections.body: Harp’s annual financial disclosure identifies Trump, of Palm Beach, Florida, as the source of a $45,000 entry described as a “Cash gift for the holidays.” The form lists Harp as a special assistant and executive assistant to the president, appointed in January 2025 as non-career executive-branch personnel. CBS News described Martin as a communications adviser, Harris as deputy director of Oval Office Operations and Nauta as director of Oval Office Operations.

sections.heading: White House disputes compensation characterization
sections.body: White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said the payments were gifts, not compensation, had no connection to the aides’ official duties and were allowed under applicable legal and ethical standards. Federal law bars executive-branch employees from receiving private salary or salary supplementation as compensation for government service. Ethics regulations permit gifts from an employee’s official superior, but define that term to exclude the president and vice president.

unresolved.text: The disclosures state the donor, description and value of the payments but do not provide a specific payment date. The public filings also do not independently establish the payments’ purpose; whether a payment is a gift or compensation depends on facts beyond its label.
The reporting and disclosures reviewed do not identify a public ethics inquiry, planned administrative action or a response from any of the four recipients.

related_stories.title: Conflicting Court Rulings Create Chaos Over Missouri's Congressional Map
related_stories.summary: A federal judge has ruled that Missouri should proceed with a new congressional map favoring Republicans, following a decision by the U.S. Supreme Court to uphold a state court ruling that directed the use of an older map. This situation has led to confusion and potential impacts on the upcoming midterm elections, as the Missouri Supreme Court has also ordered a contempt hearing regarding the secretary of state's compliance with redistricting orders.
